question: Article 34(2) of Law 2963/2001, as amended by Article 73 of Law 4850/2021, lays down restrictions on the location of private roadworthiness inspection centres (KTEO), forbidding or substantially limiting their establishment in areas within the town/city limits.

There have been complaints about these restrictions artificially reducing the availability of suitable real estate, about them making it harder for new businesses to enter the market and about them favouring existing businesses. Meanwhile, the need for these restrictions has not been substantiated.

The fact that the services provided by modern roadworthiness inspection centres are lownuisance and that they can operate under strict technical and environmental requirements, calls into question the compatibility of the contentious restrictions with Articles 49 and 56 TFEU, as well as with Articles 14 and 15 of Directive 2006/123/EC on services, which forbid unjustified geographical restrictions and require national restrictions to be necessary and proportionate.
In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it consider these provisions to be compatible with Directive 2006/123/EC and the fundamental freedoms of the internal market?
Has it assessed whether these restrictions are necessary and proportionate?
Does it intend to examine whether the application of Greek legislation constitutes an infringement of EU law and does it intend to initiate the applicable procedures if necessary?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2026) According to the Court of Justice of the European Union’s settled interpretation in Case C168/14, Grupo Itevelesa1, vehicle roadworthiness testing activities constitute ‘services in the field of transport’ within the meaning of Article 2(2)(d) of Directive 2006/123/EC (‘Services Directive’)2. As such, they fall outside the material scope of that Directive.

The EU legislation on roadworthiness testing3 leaves a certain discretion to Member States as regards the organisation of roadworthiness testing, and in particular does not regulate where testing centres should be established. Whilst in some Member States public bodies are responsible for roadworthiness testing, in others such tests are carried out by authorised private bodies.

However, it should be noted that Directive 2014/45/EU does contain certain minimum requirements concerning roadworthiness facilities (Annex III), notably as regards adequate space for the evaluation of vehicles in safe conditions.
In these circumstances, the Commission has no information to suggest that the measures referred to by the Honourable Member constitute unlawful restrictions which should be further investigated.
1 Case C-168/14 Grupo Itevelesa SL and Others v OCA Inspección Técnica de Vehículos SA and Generalidad de

Cataluña EU:C:2015:685, para 54. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/123/oj/eng. 3 Directive 2014/45/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 3 April 2014 on periodic roadworthiness tests for motor vehicles and their trailers and repealing Directive 2009/40/EC - https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02014L0045-20230520.
